title: Fair Allocation Over Time, with Applications to Content Moderation

problem.claim: The paper studies the short-term planning problem of allocating human content reviewers across harmful content categories, including allocation over time.

gap.claim: Traditional fair-allocation models do not directly account for forecasted workload constraints, time-dependent scheduling, and the desire for smooth allocations over time.

contributions.claim: The paper applies competitive equilibrium and leximin allocation rules to content-reviewer allocation and extends fair-allocation approaches to incorporate forecasted workload, time dependence, and smoothness.
An Eisenberg-Gale-inspired formulation finds allocations that satisfy forecasted workload while fairly distributing reviewers' remaining working hours across content categories.
The proposed approaches address scheduling guidance across days and minimize staffing switches by seeking allocations that do not vary substantially over time.

stated_novelty.claim: The paper explicitly presents novel practical aspects beyond the traditional Fisher market setup and introduces new extensions for time-dependent fair allocation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that their formulation produces allocations satisfying forecasted workload while fairly allocating remaining reviewer hours across categories.
The authors report that many single-period fair-allocation properties extend to the time-dependent setting, with modifications.
The authors report demonstrating the performance of their approaches using real-world data from Meta.

narrative_sequence.summary: Content moderation is important, and efficient planning is needed because of the volume of online content.
The paper formulates allocation of human reviewers across harmful content categories as a short-term planning problem.
Fair-division tools, competitive equilibrium, and leximin rules are used, with practical extensions to the Fisher market setup.
The approach incorporates forecasted workload, fair allocation of oversupply, time-dependent scheduling, and smooth allocation over time.
The authors demonstrate performance using real-world data obtained from Meta.

unknowns: The abstract does not provide formal definitions of the allocation rules or their guarantees.
The abstract does not report quantitative experimental results, baselines, or dataset details beyond the use of real-world Meta data.
The abstract does not specify the modifications to fair-allocation properties in the time-dependent setting.
